newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: YEAREND - Asian currency regimes seen slow to change.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Asian currency regimes seen slow to change.

text.p: Asian currencies are not likely to give up their close ties to the U.S. dollar in a hurry as countries in the region continue to face shifting economic and political landscapes next year, economists say.
Most regional currencies are pegged, directly or indirectly, to the dollar and to a lesser extent the yen.
But the degree of correlation and flexibility varies widely.

While Thailand confines the baht to a narrow 0.2 percent band around the central rate determined by a basket of currencies, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has said it has no target for the U.S. dollar-Singapore dollar exchange rate.
Economists said the Indonesian rupiah, which fluctuates within a fixed band against a dollar-dominated currency basket, is expected to take the biggest steps towards increased flexibility next year.
At the other end of the spectrum, Hong Kong is not seen abandoning its peg to the dollar -- which has remained unchanged since October 1983 -- as it prepares for its July 1997 handover to China.

"The Hong Kong dollar peg is going to be of central importance to maintaining stability. It's that one area of constancy throughout the transition," said Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at research firm I.D.E.A.
Supple said the Hong Kong dollar would be underpinned by the colony's improved economic prospects and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's success in maintaining a stable exchange rate.
INDONESIA MOST LIKELY TO LOOSEN GRIP

Indonesia, by contrast, looks set to continue moving towards a freer exchange rate regime after the central bank widened its dollar-rupiah intervention band twice this year, taking it to 8.0 percent from 5.0 percent in September.
Supple said Bank Indonesia was likely to widen the band to 12 percent in the first quarter of 1997, but he added that it would have to wait until upward pressure on the rupiah subsided.
"If they widen it when the market's trying to push the rupiah higher, it would reward speculators and lead to accelerated inflows," he said.
Bank Indonesia's policy of depreciating the rupiah by 3-5 percent annually has been hampered by huge short-term capital inflows from funds attracted by the country's high interest rates this year.
But the central bank has stepped up its efforts by raising the dollar-rupiah intervention band by three to four rupiah a week since late September.

Supple said Indonesia's stated aim of accelerating its foreign debt repayment in the first quarter of 1997 would provide a window of opportunity to widen the band because debt repayment would cause some weakness in the spot rate.
But Angus Armstrong, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said recent moves to lower interest rates in Indonesia had reduced pressure to widen the band.
Bank Indonesia cut its key discount rate for short-term securities (SBPUs) by 50 basis points for all maturities on December 5.
"If the currency starts to strengthen again during the second quarter, then it's quite likely they'll widen the band, probably to just 10 percent," Armstrong noted.
THAILAND STILL HURT BY POOR SENTIMENT
Thailand's efforts to move down the path to a freer forex regime are expected to be hamstrung by shaky investor confidence and a persistently large current account deficit.
"An economic recovery and revival of investor confidence would be prerequisites for any change in the Thai currency regime," said Paul Alapat, financial economist with Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong.

I.D.E.A.'s Supple said the Bank of Thailand (BOT) was unlikely to reform its forex policy until pressure on the baht eased or the current account deficit fell, despite the need for greater control of capital flows and monetary policy.
He favoured an initial doubling of the intervention band to eight satangs, but added that this was unlikely before the second half of next year.
Other analysts said the BOT was unlikely to change its forex policy in 1997 since a steady baht carrying a minimal exchange risk premium was necessary to boost confidence in the economy.

"I think it would be a mistake to change the band. If the current account improves and liquidity eases, then they might start to think about it," said a trader at one of the top four local banks in Bangkok.
Thailand's current account deficit is expected to widen to up to 8.3 percent of gross domestic product this year from 8.1 percent last year due to a slowdown in export growth.
Economists said Singapore and Malaysia had little ground to change their policy of monitoring the value of the U.S. dollar and yen in determining their exchange rates.
They said both countries, particularly Malaysia, had benefited from the appreciation of their currencies against the yen this year as this had lowered import costs.
The Taiwan dollar was also expected to remain stable after coming under severe strain during a period of tension with China earlier this year.
But economists said the Korean won could recover if the yen appreciated next year. Korea competes directly with Japan in export markets.

"They've kept the won deliberately soft in line with the yen to maintain export competitiveness this year. But Korea is typically thought to be a cyclical economy and if the world does pick up, the won could strengthen," said DMG's Armstrong.
